strengths: The paper proposes a promising application of learned edit-distance embeddings to short quaternary code construction. The integration of greedy codeword selection, embedding-based retrieval, and synchronization recovery is clearly illustrated.

The construction has a sound coding foundation: exact exclusion of radius-two Levenshtein neighborhoods ensures minimum distance at least three, permitting unique correction of one edit with an exact decoder.
Table 1 reports consistent improvements over random greedy selection across ten runs: average codebook cardinality increases by 6.4–15.8%, with a maximum improvement of 16.8% at n=11.

The neighbor-count and multiple-error ablations provide useful diagnostic evidence. Table 2 reports no failures in 100,000 sampled single-edit corrections per length with k=4. The authors also explicitly acknowledge that optimality remains conjectural and long-sequence decoding is preliminary.
weaknesses: The justification for the central density heuristic contains a technical error. Section 3.2 claims that batch normalization forces embeddings to follow a multivariate Gaussian distribution; it only normalizes moments and does not establish Gaussianity. Neither the distributional assumption nor the relationship between Gaussian density and actual neighborhood size is validated experimentally.

The headline optimality claims exceed the evidence. Matching a redundancy curve at short lengths up to n=11 establishes neither asymptotic order-optimality nor finite-length optimality. Figure 4 lacks tight cardinality bounds or exact optimization results and compares against asymptotic redundancy expressions without establishing the strongest finite-length alternatives. Labeling the conjecture honestly is appropriate, but it does not support the stronger abstract and introduction claims.

The comparisons do not adequately establish the contribution attributable to learning. Construction is compared only against random selection, without stronger combinatorial greedy heuristics or ablations of the modified loss and density ranking. Decoding is compared only against scanning the codebook; enumerating single-edit candidates and testing hash-table membership is an especially relevant exact baseline. At n=11, the reported 16.8% cardinality improvement corresponds to approximately one percentage point of code-rate improvement over random selection.

The complexity claims are insufficiently supported. Exact K-d-tree queries do not generally guarantee logarithmic time without assumptions about dimension and data distribution. The deployed k=5 decoder also performs exact edit-distance computations. Construction enumerates all 4^n strings, yet training, construction time, and memory are unreported. The acknowledged exponential DFS worst case is not accompanied by long-sequence runtime or search-size measurements.

Reliability and DNA-storage conclusions require stronger evaluation. Minimum code distance guarantees an exact decoder's correctness, but does not guarantee that the learned shortlist contains the correct codeword; zero sampled failures cannot establish this. Long-read experiments use approximately 150-nt sequences under one independent 1% equal-probability IDS model, without comparisons to practical systems such as HEDGES or DNA-Aeon. The claim that 2% RS redundancy eliminates errors needs specified block parameters and block-failure statistics, beyond average segment error rates.

Reproducibility is materially limited. The manuscript omits the instantiated base loss, embedding dimension, detailed architecture, training-pair sampling and optimization settings, treatment of variable-length inputs, exact DFS scoring and pruning rules, and RS block organization. Code is promised upon publication rather than supplied with these details. These omissions prevent independent verification of the main results. No material research-ethics concern is apparent from the synthetic-data experiments; the recommendation rests on technical support and reproducibility.
